description:
We are a team of five first-semester computer science engineering students combining basic Python programming, web design, and Gen-AI leveraging with artistic design and English communication skills.

As first-year engineering students, we combine technical curiosity with visual creativity to design accessible, well-structured space settlement concepts. By merging code, AI tool integration, and compelling visual storytelling, we aim to make space science engaging and understandable for everyone.
summary:
JANUS – The Future Space Settlement is an interactive educational game that transforms the concept of building a human settlement beyond Earth into an engaging, hands-on learning experience. Players become junior space architects, exploring possible settlement locations, assembling a rotating space habitat, and discovering how essential systems such as artificial gravity, water recycling, food production, and solar energy could support human life in space.

By turning complex space science and engineering concepts into interactive missions and challenges, JANUS makes the possibilities and challenges of space settlement easier for young learners to understand. It encourages curiosity, creativity, critical thinking, and problem-solving while introducing the importance of sustainable living beyond Earth.
As humanity continues to explore the possibility of a future among the stars, JANUS aims to inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers, and innovators to imagine, design, and contribute to that future.
details:
JANUS – The Future Space Settlement

Building Humanity’s First Home in Space

Story Behind the Project: Even though we are 17–18 years old, we only stumbled upon the concept of space settlements a few months ago. After diving deeper into how humans could live beyond Earth, our biggest thought was, "We wish we had known about this as kids." Driven by that wish , we built JANUS to bring these complex ideas to younger learners in an accessible, engaging way and sparking that curiosity without them ever having to feel like they missed out as we did.

1. Project Overview

JANUS is an interactive, web-based educational game designed to introduce children and young learners to the exciting world of space settlement design. It addresses the NASA Space Apps Challenge theme of designing a space mission by allowing players to take on the role of junior space architects and build a model of a future human habitat in space.

The idea behind JANUS is to make complex concepts in aerospace engineering, orbital mechanics, physics, and life-support systems easier to understand through interactive gameplay for kids. Instead of simply reading about how humans might live beyond Earth, players actively participate in the process of planning, designing, and assembling a space settlement.

Throughout the game, players explore possible locations for a settlement, construct its structural components, understand artificial gravity, and learn how essential resources such as oxygen, water, food, and electricity can be managed in space.

JANUS transforms the idea of a future space settlement into a step-by-step learning experience that combines science, creativity, problem-solving, and exploration.

2. Problem We Aim to Address

Space settlement is an important concept in humanity’s long-term exploration of space. However, subjects such as orbital mechanics, artificial gravity, radiation protection, habitat construction, and closed-loop life-support systems can be difficult for young learners to understand.

Most educational resources introduce these subjects through textbooks, diagrams, or technical explanations. This can make the concepts seem complicated and less engaging, particularly for students who are encountering space science for the first time.

JANUS aims to bridge this learning gap by converting these concepts into simple, visual, and interactive challenges. It encourages learners to understand the basic science behind a space settlement by experimenting with different choices and seeing how the components of a habitat fit together.

3. How JANUS Works

When players open JANUS, they are welcomed by a space-themed interface and an introductory mission screen. They can enter a player name and begin immediately without creating an account. A friendly astronaut guide accompanies the player throughout the mission, helping explain the challenges and introducing important scientific ideas.

The game is divided into three main learning levels:

LEVEL 1 – FIND THE SPOT: Orbital Mechanics

Before constructing a space settlement, players must first understand where it could be located. This level introduces orbital mechanics and the importance of selecting a suitable location for a future habitat.

Challenge 1: Choose an Orbit

Players explore different orbital altitudes and compare three possible orbital paths. They are introduced to factors such as radiation exposure, atmospheric drag, and the ease of resupplying a settlement.

Through this activity, players learn that choosing an orbit involves balancing multiple conditions rather than simply selecting the closest or highest orbit.

Challenge 2: Find a Calm Spot

Players are introduced to the Sun–Earth Lagrange points, particularly L4 and L5. They explore the positions of these points in relation to the Sun and Earth and identify suitable locations for a space settlement.

The activity introduces the idea that gravitational interactions between celestial bodies can create useful regions for placing spacecraft and other space infrastructure. It helps learners understand why Lagrange points are interesting locations for long-term space missions.

LEVEL 2 – BUILD THE WHEEL: Structural Design

After selecting a location, players move on to designing the physical structure of their settlement.

JANUS uses the concept of a Stanford Torus as inspiration for a rotating space habitat. Through drag-and-drop construction challenges, players learn how different structural components connect to form a functional settlement.

Challenge 1: Place the Hub

Players begin by placing the central hub of the settlement. The hub acts as the central connection point of the structure and provides a reference for assembling the remaining components.

Challenge 2: Build the Wheel

Players connect structural spokes to the central hub and place the torus ring around them. The spokes connect the central region to the outer habitat, while the ring represents the main living area.

This activity introduces the basic arrangement of a rotating habitat and demonstrates how the central hub, spokes, and outer ring work together as parts of one structure.

Challenge 3: Add Dock Ports

Players place docking ports at the appropriate ends of the central hub. These ports represent the locations where visiting spacecraft can connect with the settlement.

The activity introduces the importance of spacecraft docking and safe connections between a space station and visiting vehicles.

LEVEL 3 – MAKE IT HOME: Life Support and Physics

Once the basic structure is assembled, players must transform it into a place where humans could potentially live. This level introduces artificial gravity, life-support systems, food production, and energy generation.

Challenge 1: Spin for Gravity

Players use a slider to adjust the rotation speed of the settlement. The game displays the rotational speed and the corresponding simulated gravity level.

This challenge introduces the principle of artificial gravity in a rotating habitat. By rotating the settlement, people inside the outer ring would experience an apparent force directed toward the outer wall, providing a gravity-like sensation. The underlying physics is related to centripetal acceleration.

Players learn that rotation speed and habitat design are important factors when considering comfortable living conditions in space.

Challenge 2: Close the Loop

Players explore the idea of a closed-loop life-support system. The challenge introduces the importance of managing essential resources such as oxygen and water.

It demonstrates why a space settlement cannot depend entirely on continuous supplies from Earth. Instead, systems for recycling water, managing air, and reusing available resources are essential for supporting long-term human habitation.

Challenge 3: Space Farm

Players learn how food could be produced in a space habitat using hydroponic greenhouse systems. Hydroponics allows plants to grow without traditional soil by providing water and the nutrients they need.

This activity introduces the importance of sustainable food production and the role of plant-growing systems in future space settlements.

Challenge 4: Power Up

Players complete the settlement by placing solar panels on the designated mounting points. The challenge introduces solar energy as a source of electrical power for space habitats.

Players learn that solar arrays convert sunlight into electricity, which can support the settlement’s equipment, life-support systems, and daily activities.

4. Interactive Learning and Gameplay

JANUS is designed around learning through interaction rather than passive observation. Each challenge gives players an opportunity to explore a scientific concept and apply it through a simple activity.

The game includes:

  • Drag-and-drop activities: Players move orbital markers, structural components, docking ports, life-support elements, and solar panels into their appropriate positions.
  • Interactive controls: Sliders allow players to experiment with settlement rotation and observe changes in simulated gravity.
  • Instant feedback: Players receive feedback when they make a selection or place a component incorrectly, helping them understand the reasoning behind a better choice.
  • Concept explanations: Short educational prompts introduce the scientific ideas behind each activity.
  • Astronaut guidance: A friendly astronaut guide provides explanations, encouragement, and debriefs after successful challenges.
  • Progress tracking: A progress indicator and star-based scoring system encourage players to complete the mission.
  • Visual construction: As players complete challenges, they see their settlement gradually develop from an initial structure into a more complete habitat.

These features make the learning process engaging while encouraging experimentation, logical thinking, and problem-solving.

5. Mission Completion and Knowledge Assessment

After completing the construction and life-support challenges, players reach the mission completion stage. They receive a Space Architect Certificate displaying their player name, completion date, and total stars earned.

The game also includes a bonus knowledge quiz that tests the concepts introduced throughout the mission. Questions cover topics such as Low Earth Orbit, atmospheric drag, Lagrange points, artificial gravity, hydroponics, water recycling, solar energy, and space habitat design.

This final stage helps reinforce the scientific concepts learned during game play and gives players an opportunity to assess their understanding of space settlements.

6. Educational Benefits and Expected Impact

JANUS aims to make space science more accessible, enjoyable, and understandable for young learners.

Its key benefits include:

Improving STEM awareness: The game introduces fundamental concepts from science, technology, engineering, and mathematics through practical examples related to space exploration.

Encouraging systems thinking: Players discover that a successful space settlement requires several connected systems to work together. Location, structure, gravity, energy, food, air, and water all contribute to the habitability of the settlement.

Developing problem-solving skills: Interactive challenges encourage players to analyse options, make decisions, learn from mistakes, and try again.

Promoting environmental awareness: Closed-loop life-support and resource-recycling concepts introduce the importance of conserving and reusing limited resources.

Inspiring future explorers: By allowing children to experience the role of space architects, JANUS aims to encourage curiosity about aerospace engineering, astronomy, physics, and future human space exploration.

Our larger goal is to make advanced space-related ideas approachable to students who may not yet have the technical background to understand them through conventional scientific explanations.

7. Technology and Development

JANUS was developed as a browser-based interactive application using Lovable.dev as the development platform. The application is designed to be accessed through a web browser, allowing users to explore the game without requiring specialized hardware.

The project focuses on a visual and interactive user experience, including a space-themed interface, mission navigation, drag-and-drop interactions, sliders, progress tracking, star scoring, educational prompts, and a knowledge quiz.

The development approach prioritizes accessibility and ease of use so that learners can interact with the project through common internet-connected devices.

8. Future Scope

JANUS is a foundation for a larger educational space-settlement simulation. Future improvements could include more detailed habitat-design options, additional engineering challenges, expanded resource-management activities, improved scientific simulations, richer visual environments, and more advanced quizzes.

We also aim to improve the explanations provided after each challenge so that learners can understand not only what choice is correct, but also the scientific reasoning behind it.

In the future, JANUS could expand into a more comprehensive learning platform where students design, manage, and improve their own space settlements while exploring the scientific and engineering challenges involved in sustaining human life beyond Earth.

9. Conclusion

JANUS – The Future Space Settlement is more than a simple building game. It is an educational experience that introduces young learners to the challenges of designing a future human habitat in space.

By combining orbital mechanics, structural engineering, artificial gravity, closed-loop life support, hydroponic food production, and solar energy into interactive missions, JANUS makes the idea of living beyond Earth easier to explore and understand.

Our vision is to turn curiosity about space into active learning and inspire the next generation to think, design, experiment, and imagine humanity’s future among the stars.
